The “Peculiar Crimes Unit” mysteries work as standalones, but they’re kind of an acquired taste, because of the unusual methods of the octogenarian detectives (Bryant and May). While the Unit itself is kind of peculiar (staff and office always in disarray), the Unit is actually named for its mission—to investigate crimes “peculiar to London”. Thus WILD CHAMBER is about a series of murders committed in London’s parks, squares, and gardens—aka “the lungs of London” or “London’s wild chambers”.

In the novel, an elegantly dressed woman (Helen Forester) is murdered in a private garden that requires a key for admittance. Her body is discovered by a gardener, who snapped a photo of her, just moments before the killing. The photo may show her killer, caught on camera by accident, but the image is indistinct. The murder is a real “whodunit”, and more murders follow, but Bryant visits London’ parks until he is able to identify the killer. As usual, the story contains a lot of humor, mostly at the expense of the clueless PCU head (Raymond Land).

This novel includes a lot of description of London’s squares, parks, and gardens (history and monuments). Not being at all familiar with London (and not planning to visit London soon), I found this tedious. This book was slow going, even for a PCU novel, but the mystery itself was interesting enough to keep me reading to the solution at the very end.

I did love a passage about mystery writing, spoken near the novel's end by a popular writer being interviewed by Bryant: “The traditional rules of fair play demand that the criminal must be someone we’ve met. There can be no supernatural elements, no secret passages, no imaginary poisons, ..., no twins, no mystical intuitive powers, …. To them I would add several further moratoria: no more alcoholic policemen with dead wives, no autistic idiot-savant crime-scene specialists, no oppressed female detectives derided by sexist colleagues, no overweight computer nerds in dimly lit rooms, no erudite killers arranging corpses in tableaux reminiscent of medieval paintings, no renegade detectives sharing a psychic bond with the killer, no cryptic messages hidden in museums by victims, no opera-loving loners who solve mysteries because without them their lives would have no meaning, and absolutely no more reinventions of Sherlock bloody Holmes.”

Wouldn’t it be wonderful if today’s mystery novelists would abide by those rules?

Artistically inclined Robin is drawn into the mystery of the cranky old woman next door and a beautiful young girl who seems to be held against her will. Twelve-year-old Stella and her mother are refugees from Cuba, and Stella's overbearing grandmother treats her like a helpless baby because of her blindness. In defiance of her grandmother, Stella constantly wears a beautiful emerald and diamond pin in the shape of a star, a gift from her (dead) Cuban grandmother. Robin senses that more is at stake when a mysterious, unpleasant stranger shows up at the Devery house searching through rubble and sneaking around, but is preoccupied with trying to find a subject to sculpt in clay so that she can enter a sculpting class by a talented local artist.

Although dated, "Secret of the Emerald Star" is another wonderfully engaging, crisply written entry in Phyllis A Whitney's long list of excellent juvenile mysteries, which are all sadly out of print. The book makes an honest attempt to deal with ethnic and religious discrimination, a 1960s view of the Cuban crisis, and (for the time) forward thinking about dealing with blindness. The author includes a brief chapter on the inspiration for Stella's character and of her conversations with blind adolescents in preparation for writing the book, as well as the inspiration for Grandmother Devery's stuffy Staten Island neighbourhood that labels people as "Cubans," "Catholics," and "Jews."

CAT GOT YOUR DIAMONDS is an entertaining cozy mystery, by an author who thoroughly understands the genre. It's the first novel in the "Kitty Couture" series--even though there are precious few cats. Mostly the "couture" involves costumes for dancing dogs, performing chickens, and charity-connected llamas. Presumably the subsequent series entries will feature more cats (including amateur detective Lacy Crocker's cat Penelope).

In the novel, Lacy has returned to her hometown (New Orleans), in order to pursue her dream career as a designer of high-fashion costumes for pets. In her shop on historic Magazine Street ("Furry Godmother"), Lacy sells clever pet costumes and accessories, as well as home-baked pet treats made from real, healthy ingredients.

Lacy has extensive connections with the wealthy, socialite families of New Orleans, but wants to make it on her own. Thus she is seriously short of operating funds for Furry Godmother. When a hipster/derelict/criminal type (Miguel/Tony) burglarizes the shop, with Lacy inside, she sprays him with gold glitter and escapes out the back. When she returns with the police, Miguel is dead from head trauma, and Lacy is arrested (temporarily) for murder.

The arrest causes Lacy's White Knight investor to withdraw his financial support--and makes it imperative that she clear her name asap. Her amateur investigations hamper the real murder inquiry being conducted by a drop-dead gorgeous detective (Jack); and the love interest and plot events develop from there.

This is a well-plotted, entertaining cozy, if you can get past the concept of a heroine who makes her living by selling fashion costumes and treats for the pampered pets of wealthy New Orleans socialites. (Fortunately, the cozy mystery is a forgiving genre.) If you own a cat or dog, your pet may appreciate the included recipes for "Pawlines" and "Tiny Tuna Tarts".

THE ORPHAN MASTER'S SON: A NOVEL won the 2013 Pulitzer Prize for fiction, for good reason. The story grabs you, and holds you, even as you're horrified by the fact-based depiction of certain aspects of life in North Korea. Yes, there was a famine (the Arduous March (1994-1998)); yes, there were kidnappings of Japanese citizens (1977-1983); yes, there are stiff penalties for mishandling the mandatory portraits of North Korean leaders.

How could anyone choose life in North Korea, you ask yourself, as, for example, you witness Pak Jun Do's returning, repeatedly and unquestioningly, to North Korea from Japan. But then you realize that North Korea is Jun Do's country, the place where he was born, the totalitarian state with the only customs he knows and is totally familiar with.

I bought this book having never seen it before, based solely on the description given on the back cover of it. This book advertises itself as a guide for addressing errors in thought.

While he describes this system of thought to some degree, he covers it much more completely in his book "Reassess Your Chess."
The author takes a most excellent approach in presentation by taking a game that demonstrates the point he is trying to convey, and then showing how various weaker players attempted to continue the game from a certain point. As is true in his other books, Silman does tend to be very condescending in his tone. Some readers might not like this.

This EPSON RUNSENSE SF-110 GPS WATCH/ACTIVITY MONITOR is a runner's watch, not really an activity monitor. Yes, it records my steps when I wear it, and the app lets me track my weight and other things, but the watch doesn't monitor my sleep, periods of activity/inactivity, or heart rate. The watch is obviously intended primarily for tracking and analyzing running workouts (times and lap times).

INSTRUCTIONS AND SOFTWARE. Unfortunately, the instructions for using the watch are extremely confusing to figure out. For example, to use the chronograph, you must press a complex sequence of buttons on the watch itself. Specifically, the button steps are: (1) press D from the Time screen to display Menu; (2) press C/D to highlight Workout, then press A; (3) press C on the Measurement screen to start measuring; (4) press D while measuring to record a lap; (5) press C again to stop measuring; (6) press D while measuring to display Measure Menu screen; (7) press C/D to highlight Stop Workout, then press A. Did you get all that?

In several sessions, I have tried to record a walking workout, but I've been unable to successfully start and stop a single one. Worse, when I connect the watch to my PC, and ask the app to upload my watch data, it always returns the message: "There is no data to upload". This is true even though the watch has been recording my steps, and I can see my step activity by pressing an entirely different, equally complex sequence of watch buttons.

Regarding the software/app, my first mistake was to try to begin using the watch via the Android cellphone app. The app works, but the Runsense software display is far more complete and easier to understand when you connect the watch and its cradle to a PC.

Maybe I'm spoiled, because I have a [[ASIN:B00GOGV314 Jawbone UP24]] that tracks my steps, sleep, times of activity and inactivity, weight, and workout times through an easy-to-use cellphone app that uploads data automatically whenever the phone is connected to a wireless or cellphone network. My specific Jawbone model has been discontinued, but there are newer models that do everything mine does, and also track heart rate. I'm sure that these newer models are equally easy to use.

GPS MAPPING FEATURE. The reason I ordered this Epson Runsense watch, when I already owned a reliable activity tracker, was that I wanted the GPS feature that is supposed to map and calculate the routes and distances travelled in workouts. However, the Runsense SF-110 can hardly ever locate a GPS signal for me, and repeatedly returns the message "Failed" .

The instructions say that the GPS feature requires being somewhere with no overhead obstructions--which I guess means you have to be outdoors. However, when I go outdoors and press the buttons for "GPS location", the watch can't find a signal. So no maps, no distances for me! I do live in a hilly area, but my cellphone and tablets are always able to find GPS locations easily, even indoors.

TIME KEEPING. The watch has a large, easy-to-read time display, and it keeps good time. There is a button that lights up the time display when you press it. The plastic watchband is attractive and has a gazillion little holes, so it will fit any size wrist without resizing.

BLUETOOTH PAIRING. The watch was easy to pair with my Samsung Galaxy S4 cellphone.

It is possible that my EPSON RUNSENSE SF-110 GPS WATCH/ACTIVITY MONITOR is a defective lemon, given that I can't get the GPS or the data upload features to work. However, even if those worked, I would still find the button-pushing sequences too complex to be useable on a daily basis. Consequently, I rate this product at 1 star ("I hate it" on the official Amazon scale).

The last time I selected a Christmas devotional I came away disappointed. The author of that devotional was more interested in pushing an agenda that ran counter to Christian faith and was more about self-justification than honoring Jesus - the real purpose behind Christmas. On that basis I was very reluctant to select another devotional out of concern of finding another self-serving justification for moral bankruptcy. Fortunately, the author of Total Christmas Makeover is very much on target and has one agenda in her delightful devotional - focus on Jesus and bring Christmas back into proper context. This has turned out to be one of the better Christmas devotionals I have seen.

Every single day begins with a passage of Scripture reading from the Bible. This is followed by a short devotional text, usually from the author’s life experiences or observations, and followed with a short prayer. This is a tried-and-true format and there’s nothing unusual here. After the prayer section, the author includes a handful of questions that are thought-provoking but not aggressive. The questions are useful not only for personal reflection and meditation but can be used in a small group for family study as well. Finally, some days end with a “practical application” section that are suggestions on putting the day’s discussion into practice. Overall, this is a successful formula for a devotional.

Though there are 31 daily readings, these are broken up into three groups: Ritual, Relationships, and Rest, all of which are useful for personal growth. The breakdown seems to be very logical and thought out.

So, what makes this particular devotional worth your time investment? Unlike the last devotional I tried to work through, every single day’s reading is focused on Jesus and putting the attention on Him. There’s no fluff ‘n stuff, no commercialism, no alternative viewpoints for consideration, just a steady, gentle guiding back to Jesus and the reason Christmas is a celebration about Him and nothing else. The readings are easy and gentle, non-confrontational and all are relatively short.

The subtitle is “31 Devotions to Celebrate With Purpose” and that’s on target. That purpose is focusing on Jesus, the real reason behind Christmas. Seeing friends and family, exchanging gifts and having nice dinners are all nice things but it’s easy to get lost in the details. This little devotional helps the reader refocus and remember why we do all of those things. This is a devotional I will be breaking out to share with my wife every December.

Corbett journeys back to North Carolina to solve a murder on a plantation. Brilliant writing, compelling prose and the historical setting so vividly portrayed made this a winner for me.

BOOK #1 SPEAKS THE NIGHTBIRD - Judgment of the Witch The Carolinas, 1699: The citizens of Fount Royal believe a witch has cursed their town with inexplicable tragedies -- and they demand that beautiful widow Rachel Howarth be tried and executed for witchcraft. Presiding over the trial is traveling magistrate Issac Woodward, aided by his astute young clerk, Matthew Corbett. Believing in Rachel's innocence, Matthew will soon confront the true evil at work in Fount Royal.... Evil Unveiled - After hearing damning testimony, magistrate Woodward sentences the accused witch to death by burning. Desperate to exonerate the woman he has come to love, Matthew begins his own investigation among the townspeople. Piecing together the truth, he has no choice but to vanquish a force more malevolent than witchcraft in order to save his beloved Rachel -- and free Fount Royal from the menace claiming innocent lives.

BOOK #2 THE QUEEN OF BEDLAM - takes Matthew Corbett, to New York circa 1700, where a killer wields a bloody and terrifying power over a bustling city carving out its identity -- and over Matthew's own uncertain destiny. The unsolved murder of a respected doctor has sent ripples of fear throughout a city teeming with life and noise and commerce. Who snuffed out the good man's life with the slash of a blade on a midnight street? The local printmaster has labeled the fiend "the Masker," adding fuel to a volatile mystery...and when the Masker claims a new victim, hardworking young law clerk Matthew Corbett is lured into a maze of forensic clues and heart-pounding investigation that will both test his natural penchant for detection and inflame his hunger for justice. In the strangest twist of all, the key to unmasking the Masker may await in an asylum where the Queen of Bedlam reigns -- and only a man of Matthew's reason and empathy can unlock her secrets. From the seaport to Wall Street, from society mansions to gutters glimmering with blood spilled by a deviant, Matthew's quest will tauntingly reveal the answers he seeks -- and the chilling truths he cannot escape.

BOOK #3 MISTER SLAUGHTER - 1702 New York City takes Matthew and the reader on an unforgettable journey of horror, violence, and personal discovery. The journey begins when Matthew, now an apprentice "problem solver" for the London-based Herrald Agency, accepts an unusual and hazardous commission. Together with his colleague, Hudson Greathouse, he agrees to escort the notorious mass murderer Tyranthus Slaughter from an asylum outside Philadelphia to the docks of New York. Along the way, Slaughter makes his captors a surprising - and extremely tempting - offer. Mister Slaughter is at once a classic portrait of an archetypal serial killer and an exquisitely detailed account of a fledgling nation still in the process of inventing itself.

BOOK #4 THE PROVIDENCE RIDER - the winter of 1703, with Matthew still haunted by his lethal encounter with notorious mass murderer Tyranthus Slaughter. When an unexplained series of explosions rocks his Manhattan neighborhood, Matthew finds himself forced to confront a new and unexpected problem. Someone is trying--and trying very hard--to get his attention. That someone is a shadowy figure from out of Matthew's past: the elusive Dr. Fell. The doctor, it turns out, has a problem of his own, one that requires the exclusive services of Matthew Corbett. The ensuing narrative moves swiftly and gracefully from the emerging metropolis of New York City to Pendulum Island in the remote Bermudas. In the course of his journey, Matthew encounters a truly Dickensian assortment of memorable, often grotesque, antagonists. These include Sirki, the giant, deceptively soft-spoken East Indian killer, Dr. Jonathan Gentry, an expert in exotic potions with a substance abuse problem of his own, the beautiful but murderous Aria Chillany, and, of course, the master manipulator and 'Emperor of Crime' on two continents, Dr. Fell himself. The result is both an exquisitely constructed novel of suspense and a meticulous recreation of a bygone era. Filled with danger, narrative surprises, and an almost tangible sense of place, The Providence Rider is historical fiction at its finest and most developed. It is the novel that McCammon's many devoted readers have been waiting for. They will not be disappointed.

NIGHTTOWN (A JUNIOR BENDER MYSTERY) is the 7th novel in the amusing “Junior Bender” series, and it works as a standalone. Junior (that's his given name) is a professional burglar--and a very good one, because he was mentored in “the art of the steal” by master burglar Herbie Mott. Thanks to Herbie, Junior lives by an ethical code that's saved him many sleepless nights--the first rule being “never take the best thing they own”.

In the novel, Junior needs money to help out his girlfriend Ronnie, so he warily accepts a job that's offering too much money for the task. The client wants him to enter an empty house, using a supplied house key, and retrieve a doll left there by the recently deceased owner. That's it. For $25,000 now, and $25,000 after delivery of the doll.

Exercising his usual abundance of caution, Junior arrives for the job on the day AFTER the client expected him. He finds another burglar--a friend of his--in the house, and the friend already has the doll. But it's been cut open, and when the friend delivers the doll to the client, she is murdered.

Junior sets out to avenge her, even though it puts the lives of Ronnie, his daughter, his divorced wife, and himself in danger. Junior must cash in all of the accumulated favors owed him by his criminal underworld and Hollywood movie industry contacts, in order to identify and take out all of the people behind the disastrous “easy” job.

Whenever a new Junior Bender novel arrives, I can't wait to read it. Author Timothy Hallinan is a master of the comic mystery, and other reviewers’ comparisons of his novels to those of Raymond Chandler and Donald Westlake are NOT exaggerated.

I was taken aback by the title of this book and at the same time intrigued when I first saw it. I was unsure what was meant by “cultural Christianity” though something about it seemed familiar. It turns out that I knew what cultural Christianity is but didn’t really have a name for it. In addition to putting a name to a situation I have seen lived out several times over the years, this book aims to give the reader some ideas on how to help others see where they’ve just been going through the motions. It’s a good resource for identifying where people call themselves Christians without actually living it out, and it does offer some guidance on how to break through and reach these people.

The author defines cultural Christianity by identifying many different groups of people who identify themselves as Christians but are so in name only. These groups include people who are religious but not faithful, people who identify church membership as being Christian, those that equate Christianity with observing traditions, people who believe that being a “good person” is sufficient, and more. Each of these groups has its unique issues, but they all have one thing in common: they have a false view of Christianity and salvation. Though the core issue is the same the reasons behind the issue are varied and by breaking these down into categories the author makes it easier to understand what’s going on.

Chapter 4, “Bridging the Gap”, covers how to have conversations intended to challenge people who have their focus on the wrong things and have a misunderstanding of what it truly means to be a Christian. It explains how to find a starting point or common ground and how to ask some tough questions without starting a hostile disagreement. It even offers up some questions to ask.

This book is set up with questions for discussion at the end of each chapter. This makes this a possible resource for small group study.

A good many people who call themselves Christians do not understand that they’re mistaken. This book is designed to help the reader first understand where they themselves are, and then provide insight on how to reach others and help them find the path to a proper Christian perspective. This is a sorely needed resource.

I discovered this cookbook on the shelf of a store that specializes in used books and I grabbed it while I had the chance to do so. It looked like a good collection with easy-to-prepare recipes that would greatly expand the dishes I put in front of my family. This cookbook has exceeded my expectations and I have come to regard it as the best Italian cookbook I own.

This is a thick book, over 400 pages of recipes and directions. The collection is broken up into the following categories: Appetizers, Soups & Salads, Side Dishes, Meats, Poultry & Fish, Meatless Pasta Main Dishes, Pizza & Sandwiches, Classic Dishes, 25-Minute Main Dishes, Slow-Cooker Recipes and finally Desserts. There are also a couple of chapters that provide good supplementary information, tips, substitutions and conversion charts.

This is a softcover book with the plastic comb binding, which allows it to lay flat when on the counter. This is a good thing as it means less wear and tear on the binding. The formatting of each recipe is consistent - a readable typeface in pleasant shades of red and green, with prep times and nutritional information and step-by-step directions that are clear and concise. I have yet to find a recipe in this cookbook that is hard to understand or follow.

With very few exceptions the recipes make good use of convenient items such as canned tomato sauce, pre-made Italian style meatballs and the like. The items used in the recipes are the kinds of things that many households will already have on hand which makes having Italian meals for dinner a lot easier. I have seen countless cookbooks that require a trip to an ethnic or specialty grocer - this is not the case with this cookbook.

This is all good, but if the recipes aren't good then a cookbook isn't worth the paper on which it's printed. So far, the recipes I have tried have turned out well. In particular, we have found that Spaghetti Pie is a family favorite and is suitable for company. Skillet Lasagna is another big hit with the family and it's so easy and fast to make that we can have dinner on the table in 45 minutes or less, start to finish. I have a number of other recipes that I have not yet tried that are on my list of dishes to make in the next several weeks.

This is a great Italian cookbook! It is a great collection of good recipes, all easy to prepare and most are fast to the table. If you like Italian food and you don't want to work too hard to get it, then this cookbook is for you. It's out of print now, so the best option is to find a used copy online (or in a bookstore that sells used cookbooks).

As a side note, after I got home with the copy I bought in the bookstore I made the unfortunate discovery that someone had torn out a couple of pages. So, I have ordered another copy.

Has finally been demystified in the lighthearted (and uber-delicious) "The Book of Buns" by Jane Mason, the author of [[ASIN:1849752575 All You Knead Is Bread: Over 50 Recipes from Around the World to Bake & Share]]. Hint: it's not the gym. From page 9: "If you want firm buns, go to the gym. The joy of buns is the fluffy, soft squishiness of them." And the book's dedication: "To Enrique who loves my buns."

Containing over 50 recipes for various types of sweet and savory buns from (virtually) every corner of the globe, you'll be sure to make several tasty new discoveries that will make their way into your regular baking rotation. Not surprisingly, many of the recipes are European; hot cross buns, saffron buns, Chelsea buns and Lincolnshire plum buns from the UK, numerous sweet buns from Switzerland, Norway, Hungary, and Armenia, pirozhki and bublik from Eastern Europe, and plenty of crusty German rolls to round things out. Latin America is also well represented, with recipes from Mexico, Peru, Uruguay, and El Salvador. The Middle East/ Africa offers numerous buns such as ka'ak (Syria), khubza bil ashab (Libya), khubz mahala and bun muska (Iran), khubz mbassis (Tunisia), meloui (Morocco), and shubbak el-habayeb (Iraq). You'll also find Montreal-style bagels and monkey bread from North America. There is truly something for everyone represented here!

Ingredients (both metric and volume) and instructions are very clearly laid out, and a helpful guide to ingredients, working with dough, and basic shaping and filling techniques will get you started on the right foot. Each recipe is illustrated with a photo of the finished bun, and many feature numbered step-by-step photos as well, which are tremendously helpful for the more involved recipes. All of these recipes freeze well and can be reheated quickly in the microwave or oven.

The first recipe I tried was the Lebanese sfoof, a beautiful yellow bun twisted into elegant rings and sprinkled with chopped pistachios. The addition of mahlab, anise seeds, and orange blossom water give these a delicate spice; due to the 30 minutes of hand kneading, they are moist and fluffy and go excellently with Turkish coffee.

The second recipe I tried was the bastounakia (literally "salt sticks,") a sourdough-ish Greek breadstick made with plenty of chopped fresh rosemary. I also brushed mine with [[ASIN:B004HIZ7HW Amoretti Premium Organic Extra Virgin finishing Olive Oil Infused with the Natural Flavor & Aroma of Kalamata Olives - 500ml Bottle]] and Cornish sea salt that took these over the top. These would pair well with any salad or soup.

The third recipe I tried as the dolce Milanese, a sweet layered bun filled with a pound of raisins (I threw together the remnants of my dried fruit, so mine was a mix of currants, golden raisins, and regular raisins). I should have done a better job draining the raisins (including patting them off with paper towels), because I found the dough unpleasantly wet to work with during the several rounds of folding in the fruit. However, the final bread was moist and flaky (if a little heavy from all the fruit!) and froze well.

I also made several of the Asian-inspired recipes including the coconut buns from China (you will also find several variations on Chinese steamed dumplings) and Japanese anpan. Having lived in Japan, I am addicted to anpan and other sweet buns (red beans, green tea, and red bean paste are frequent ingredients in Japanese pastry), and enjoyed making my own at home. I have bookmarked numerous other recipes to try, including the amazing Bulgarian layered cheese bread tootmanik s gotovo testo, masala buns from India, Moroccan krachel, and South African chocolate sticks.

Some general observations: I baked all my buns on a Silpat, and I turned down the heat quite a bit from what was recommended (I tend to bake most of my breads at 350, and perhaps a few minutes at 375 to brown; many of the buns here call for temps as high as 400-425). Also, the author tends to use a lot of salt; I am sensitive to salt, so I cut the recommended amount in half. The bastounakia calls for 2 - 2.5 tsp. for only 16 breadsticks, for example. There is no salt in the dough for this particular recipe, so I went with a light hand when sprinkling the breadsticks. You can also use sourdough in place of yeast; the author gives detailed recommendations for substituting rye- and wheat-based starters for the yeast.

One great bonus is the fact that you will develop the arms of a stevedore after hand-kneading all these doughs; I'm a firm believer in hand-kneading over a stand mixer as it gives you a much better "feel" for when the dough is ready. It is also a great workout for your arms!

Overall, "The Book of Buns" is a great way to try out sweet and savory bread recipes from around the world in a portable (and freezable!) format. There is plenty of variety to keep you baking happily for many weeks / months to come; if you try one bun recipe a week, you can pretty much get a year's worth of bakes! The clear lists of ingredients, instructions, and directions (and the helpful step-by-step photos) make this approachable by any level of baker, and there are very little specialty flours / ingredients required (with the exception of mahlab and orange blossom water), so you should be able to locate ingredients at your local supermarket. I strongly suggest purchasing a Silpat if you do not already own own; it has revolutionized my bread baking and makes cleanup a snap, plus it is reusable for hundreds of uses.

Good luck and happy baking!

This is not a great book; it is an INCREDIBLE book. Although, it is geared predominantly toward outlining the soft skills necessary for becoming a successful and influential project manager, these skills are applicable to anyone in any job or in everyday life. I believe anyone can achieve success with these methods.

Project managers operate without any formal authority, so they use informal power by influencing team members and other stakeholders. There are many traits that enable a project manager to gain influence over time such as by being authentic (say what you mean) and acting with integrity (do what you say). Trust is of utmost importance and that has to be earned. Mentoring is another level of influence and so is the act of influencing others who then become a positive influence for someone else (this type of influence has a multiplying effect).

This book is 179 pages of easy reading written in a conversational style that guides the reader on how to gain the power of influence. This advice can be applied to other professions as well. For example, in the develop commitment chapter, the author says "Persuasion encourages someone to do something once. Influence is about encouraging them to keep on doing something and to keep on supporting you." In that chapter he describes how that is done in several ways. The hook is one way to start influencing someone we never met. He goes on to describe three hooks that work for him. When I was reading his example, it brought to mind the hook I used about 12 years ago when I was trying to raise $1,900 for a 60-mile breast cancer walk. I thought this was impossible at the time but I made a pact with myself that since this would be the only time I would ever raise a large sum of money I would give it my all. With this in mind, I decided to contact every acquaintance I knew and some I did not know. I wrote each one a brief email that established a personal connection with them by reminding them how we knew each other or how I came upon their name. Then I told them my goal and asked for a donation. I figured most people would ignore a bulk email but not an individual one and I was right. In the end, 91 people donated a total of $5,470 to sponsor me which does not include the $550 in donations made by 2 other acquaintances who donated to a different breast cancer organization in my name. In total I was able to raise $6,020. It was the hook I used that allowed me to influence most of the people I wrote including several who I never met and who never met me. When the walk was done, I sent a handwritten card and a story I wrote about the event to thank each of the 91 sponsors. I even attached a picture of me in those cards I sent to the people who I never met so that they would see who they had supported. The hook got them listening and the thank you helped them remember and established a rapport. Hooks are used by sales representatives as an influencing tactic and this example can be seen as selling someone on a cause.

On another note, there are brief scoring exercises at the end of each chapter that I used to rate my influencing skills. A couple of exercises I found confusing. For example, in the active listening chapter it is unclear to me how I was supposed to use my scores because the author mentions they had to be broken down into five dimensions, yet the questions were not broken down by those dimensions.

I do think this book is way overpriced at the current price of $38.84 even though the advice is excellent. Personally, I would not pay more than $23 for this small text. Nevertheless, this book will help most people understand and acquire the soft skills necessary for becoming a successful project manager or successful "anybody." I found it to be an incredible read with outstanding and sensible advice.

Stove pipe hats off to Louis Bayard for this unique and beguiling perspective of the early years of one of America’s most beloved Presidents Abraham Lincoln. The story is cleverly written through the eyes of the two people closest to him: a young politically minded Mary Todd and his beloved friend and roommate Joshua Speed.

The novel begins in 1839 and takes place mostly before Lincoln became president. It is told solely from Mary and Speed’s perspectives, both of whom paint Mr Lincoln in a sometimes unflattering, but always very humble and human light.

Joshua Speed is Lincoln’s landlord, friend and through circumstance, bedmate – beds being hard to come by for poor bachelors like Lincoln and therefore often having to be shared. They become fast friends and to many on-lookers almost like an old married couple, often finishing each other’s sentences and telling stories in perfect synchronicity. Speed always has in his mind that he and Lincoln will remain eternal bachelors together until a would-be matchmaker reminds Lincoln that any aspiring politician needs a wife. When Lincoln meets the enigmatic and politically minded Mary Todd, Speed realizes all he is about to lose.

Mary Todd is a sharp-witted and fiery woman with a mind for politics, which is something we are not used to seeing given most accounts paint her as a melancholy and difficult. Panicked by the thought of “entering the vale of spinsterhood,” at age twenty she travels from Kentucky to her sister and brother-in-laws’s home in Springfield with the “grim and single-minded resolve” of landing herself a husband. There she will meet the awkward and socially inept man of few words, Abraham Lincoln. One can definitely say that it’s not love at first sight for the pair, but as with all great love stories, it takes time to grow.

As Mary starts to get noticed in Springfield, a young Lincoln makes fumbling attempts to woo her guided by advice from his “dandy” friend Joshua Speed. Once Mary and Abraham get past the early obstacles (some caused by Speed), they begin to steal away for “unchaperoned tête-à-têtes,” but when their liaisons are discovered, the upper society of Springfield is scandalized by their secret engagements.

Bayard, as with all his novels, is the master of suspense. And even though many of us know how the story ends it still will keep you on the edge of your seat from the first to the last page. “Courting Mr Lincoln” is a truly moving novel about three extraordinary people and how their lives intertwined for better or for worse.

This tale is full of art forgeries, abductions, lingering grief, psychological manipulation, ghoulish entities, revenge, and loads of malevolent intent! A high-octane ride throughout; readers will be engrossed.

This story is intended to be more entertaining than it is meant to be authentically realistic, so an open-minded sense of perspective and interpretation is required to find the enjoyment it can provide.

THE ANOMALY is a rather pedestrian ancient-cave-exploration thriller about a fifth-rate-documentary-filming team’s discovery of actual buried secrets. The irony of it all is that afterwards the team can’t tell anyone about the discovery. Again and again, the author absolutely nails the phony on-screen dialogue spewed by the on-camera “explorer” (Nolan). For example, “Will we find the cavern? I don’t know. But I do know this: in the search for truth, it matters not whether we find. It matters only that we continue to seek.”

I hate those empty reality documentaries that air all the time on cable channels, so I didn’t enjoy reading Nolan’s glib pronouncements one bit. However, the Nolan character himself isn’t bad--Nolan and his producer (Ken) are both cynically aware of the emptiness of the documentaries that they make to sell to a gullible public.

The plot takes off from a real April 1909 newspaper story (reproduced in the novel) about a cavern supposedly discovered in the Grand Canyon by explorer G.E. Kincaid. The story has all the stock elements of an archaeological thriller: a huge stone rolling down a passageway, explorers trapped by blockage of the only exit, discovery of mysterious writings, emergence of frightening creatures, secret society conspiracy, and so on. Some of the film team members live, some don’t.

This is a rather slow-moving novel, and I just couldn’t warm to it. It’s okay if you like any and all thrillers belonging to the “Indiana Jones” genre.

The War Before the War is a fascinating study of the controversy of holding men and women in slavery. Extremely detailed, full of politics, human nature, legal viewpoint and greed. It was a well rounded view of all points for and against slavery which lead to the split of America and the ensuing civil war.

Especially interesting was the breath of information on slaves, Ex-slaves, fear, and the reasoning of many leaders who felt that slavery must remain for the society to have a solid foundation. The theory was that every society needed a low level work force under the poor whites in order to buffer them from being lower on the caste system.

The book also expounds on the reason for many pushing to remove freed slaves back to Africa. So many interesting points, reference to many groups organized to uplift ex-slaves, and run away slaves. You will hear from so many men responsible for making the hard decisions, trying to placate their constituents, neighbors, and reverse the constitutional right to being born free. Brilliant, necessary, and a great read!

I have worked with a large number of computers by various manufacturers, and I can say that each one has had its strengths and weaknesses. I was really intrigued by this one with the 8th generation i3 chip – I didn’t even realize that the i3 was still being developed or produced. My experience with this laptop (and its chip) has been a mix of positive and negative, though the positive does outweigh the negatives I see.

I will start by addressing the elephant in the room. This system comes with only 4GB of DDR4 RAM. Why? The standard anymore is 8GB unless all you’re doing is surfing the web and writing documents. I am not sure what possessed Dell to release a machine with that little RAM running Windows 10. So, my first order of business was popping the case open and expanding to 8GB, which was easy with a single 8GB stick. There are two slots in there, and 8GB works in one slot, so I am hopeful I can bump it to 16GB.

While I was in there, I was in for a surprise. There is a hard drive bay, and it’s empty. The system registers 256GB in a solid state flash, which is elsewhere (I did not see it but I know it's in there).

Oddly enough, the Dell software does not recognize the increased RAM though Windows and the system BIOS definitely see it. That’s a minor issue, not a real concern. It does need to be kept in mind though – it could be confusing for the unaware.

This is an UltraBook system, meaning that some shortcuts were taken to keep things light and small. The main thing missing is a CD/DVD drive which is hit or miss on UltraBooks. There is HDMI for video output but no other video output interfaces. Surprisingly, there is no USB type C port, but there are three type A ports. There is also an audio jack and an Ethernet port, as well as an SD card reader. The power button doubles as a fingerprint reader.

I booted the system, set it up and was on the network downloading updates within about 10 minutes. I was presented with a fairly clean desktop and not too much extra fluff n’ stuff. The system was a bit sluggish for the first hour as things were updated and cached, but it has settled down now and things are reasonably peppy. I have done little with the graphics beyond loading a video and looking at image files, though I expect it will handle light gaming and graphics work like photo editing, though the latter would definitely benefit from having 8GB instead of 4.

Windows did not activate automatically and I needed to run the troubleshooter before it activated. I am not sure what went wrong there, but it was a temporary issue and very quickly and easily resolved. I suspect there was a network issue.

The screen is slightly less bright than that of my Acer and Toshiba systems, though that’s not necessarily a bad thing. The screen is not as harsh to look at, and the resolution is good, so I would consider this a plus. Pictures and image files look clear and sharp with good color.

The real surprise is the sound, which is much better than I expected and is great for watching videos without requiring headphones or speakers. I will still use BT output when I want to listen to anything important (music or a movie), but the built-in speakers are more than adequate.

I chose this book for several reasons: I speak Spanish, I studied several other Hispanic young adult novels such as [[ASIN:014038068X An Island Like You: Stories of the Barrio]], [[ASIN:044970436X Cool Salsa]], [[ASIN:0142302090 Journey of the Sparrows]], [[ASIN:0380732475 Lupita Manana (Harper Trophy Books)]], and [[ASIN:0141306432 Felita]], and I live in a city with a Hispanic majority, so I was interested in reading these Latino monologues aimed at teens.

First of all, the monologues were all written by adults, and the majority of the characters all *sound* like adults attempting to recapture youth. Not many teens would defend their Latino roots with "some sort of familiar foundation is being sought and a sense of community kinship is forming." Another is a nod to Kafka; a boy dreams of turning into a chicken after consuming it voraciously in every shape and form. Or the girl who muses that "Venus...is the lantern of dawn. After naming the stars, I caress the spines of my books."

My main issue with Voices in First Person was the lack of any real Latino theme detectable in several of the monologues; many are ripe with teenage angst that is familiar in any culture, written in a generic English that fails to be rich with Spaniglish like Judith Ortiz Cofer's works. Gary Soto's "Spending Money," Esmeralda Santiago's "I Stand At The Crosswalk," Sandra Cisneros's "Darious and the Clouds," Gwylym Cano's violent "Angel's Monologue" and Michael Mejias's sexually explicit profane rant "Mujeriego" are written in Black English, none of these have a distinctly Latin feel to their rhythms, inflections, or choice of words. The themes of suicide, child abuse, sexual attraction, teenage pregnancy, superstition and alienation could just as easily be about suburban America or in the case of "Mujeriego," tough inner-city ghetto life.

The few monologues that do deal explicitly with Latino culture (Ritual, Reclaim Your Rights as a Citizen of Here, Jose, My First American Summer, God Smells Like a Roast), Sylvia, Barrio ABCs) were the most effective. Black and white photographs grace each monologue, although the images are generic and rarely deal directly with Latino culture (the pen line drawings generally are Latino, like dancing skulls and Mexican ice cream pushcarts).

Not being a theater teacher or English teacher, I can't say if I'd let high school students perform some of these in class, partiularly the ultra-violent and sexual "Mujeriego," featuring the testimony of a Latino teenager charged with burning down a club and killing 33 people. The profanity-laced tirade features sodomy and is peppered with unprintables (at first glance, I counted about 21 profanities in the monologue's three pages), including sexually explicit terms for females and gang rape. Also, two of the works deal with suicidal intentions. The works themselves are very short; if printed on an 8 x 11 sheet of paper, these would be a page if not less, not much time to develop the supposed theme of reflections on Latino identity.

If I were looking for a book on modern Latino culture to use in a high school or college classroom, I would be much more likely to choose [[ASIN:044970436X Cool Salsa]] or [[ASIN:0805076166 Red Hot Salsa: Bilingual Poems on Being Young and Latino in the United States]] (also edited by Lori Marie Carlson); these poems are distinctly Latino in flavor, many written in Spanglish or peppered with Spanish, and include much more of a cultural element than Voices in First Person. The generic tone of the many narrators and the amount of violence (child abuse, murder, suicidal intentions) and profanity got in the way of any potentially empowering message on Latino identity in today's teenagers.

THE PATRIOT THREAT is another "Da Vinci Code" formula novel--in which the lead character embarks on a sort of treasure hunt, following a bread-crumb trail of clues (found in widely scattered documents, maps, artifacts, building decorations, whatever) to discover or protect a shocking, closely-guarded secret that will change the world if revealed. Nobody does this kind of novel better than accomplished writer Steve Berry, and nobody carries out the investigation better than Berry's well-rounded, fearless operative Cotton Malone.

In this adventure, U.S. President Danny Daniels asks the Magellan Billet (headed by Stephanie Nelle) and the Secretary of the Treasury (Joe Levy) to investigate a global insurance scam that produces an annual $20 million "birthday gift" for North Korea's head of state (Dear Leader). When this year's birthday present literally goes up in flames, Cotton's attention is drawn to Dear Leader's close relative (Kim Yong Jin). Eventually he learns that Kim Yong Jin is covertly pursuing a bundle of classified original and copied documents that a whistle-blowing former federal employee has stolen from the files of the U.S. Treasury Department.

For the most part, the documents relate to (1) the mystery of why several successive U.S. Presidents appointed Andrew Mellon as Secretary of the Treasury; (2) to the purpose of a mystery meeting that actually occurred between President Franklin Delano Roosevelt and his hated adversary Andrew Mellon; and (3) to questions surrounding the ratification of the Sixteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution (adopted in February 1913, authorizing the U.S. income tax). To obtain the stolen documents, Kim Yong Jin will stop at nothing, because he is convinced that their publication will invalidate the U.S. income tax. This will destroy the U.S. economy by obligating the U.S. government to repay all the monies, plus interest, that it has fraudulently collected from its citizens since 1913 under the authority of the invalid Amendment. Publication will also destroy most of the rest of the world's economy, including the Chinese economy, all to the benefit of North Korea's economy.

THE PATRIOT THREAT is a page-turner thriller, with lots of spy action, murders, espionage dirty tricks, cipher-breaking, and unexpected plot twists. The characters are all well drawn and memorable. I liked this new entry in the Cotton Malone series much better than the previous novel ([[ASIN:0345526570 The Lincoln Myth]]), because it doesn't include so much invented history, and doesn't play so fast and loose with actual historical facts and events.

Evidently there are genuine questions about the ratification of the Sixteenth Amendment, and the novel's argument that the Amendment's invalidation would destroy the U.S. and world economy is totally logical and rational. Of course, as a practical matter, the U.S. Courts will never declare the Sixteenth Amendment invalid, because it has been accepted as the law of the land for more than a century. But in THE PATRIOT THREAT, Steve Berry has created a fascinating, fast-moving novel that uses the idea to great advantage, without ever offending the reader's willingness to suspend disbelief.

Until fairly recently I understood "barbecue" to mean "food cooked over a fire outside". I have since come to the understanding that barbecue is more about the smoke than just the heat, and up to this point grilling was all I really understood. When I found this book second-hand in a used bookstore I snapped it up (and what it was doing in that store I am sure I will never quite understand). This book is an authoritative reference on proper barbecue method, equipment and of course recipes.

The authors start off with a good explanation of what barbecue really is and what it isn't. Like the Jamisons' other books, the introductory explanations are very thorough, clear and easy to grasp. They leave nothing for guesswork and there's no reason to walk away without a very good grasp of the basics, just by reading the very first chapter.

Included in the introductory chapters is a good summary of equipment needed for barbecue. This includes a comparison of different cooking equipment and explaining the strengths and weaknesses of each one. Additional equipment such as heat mitts, meat thermometers and more are all listed too.

Included is a collection of roughly 30 recipes for rubs, mops, glazes and sauces. This collection is not an exhaustive collection by any means, but it is a well-rounded selection of flavor enhancers that work well for all manner of foods being barbecued. One thing to keep in mind about this collection - the recipes make a lot! Other recipes collections I have seen for making rubs and sauces usually make small amounts - about a quarter cup total. These recipes make many times more in quantity and while that's ok it means figuring out what to do with the mixtures for storage or planning to use it all at once (which makes sense for the marinades but not for the rubs unless making a lot of food).

The rest of the recipes and techniques in this book are divided up into several logical sections - beef, pork, poultry, seafood and more. There are even chapters for sides and sauces to complement the barbecue. Every recipe and technique is thoroughly written out and explained in sufficient detail to remove any doubts and most questions.

There are a couple of sections at the back of the book that offer up recipes for suitable accompaniments and beverages. These additional offerings definitely fit with the collection and they do work well. I was a little surprised by the beverages section - I was not expecting to find such when I bought this book.

There is one thing about this book that I would change though it is a minor point. There's a whole section on rubs, mops and marinades, but several of the main dish recipes include their own recipes for additional rubs and glazes too. If a recipes includes such a flavor enhancer instead of in the chapter with the others of its type, it could get a little challenging to find a rub or marinade recipe for trying with a different dish. Personally, I would have liked to see a cross reference back to the rubs and marinades collection in each recipe, or at least a reference to each recipe in the chapter so that it would be easier to find later. This is a nitpick more than anything but it's worth mentioning.

Smoke and Spice is a great cookbook for anyone who is looking to make real barbecue or wants to take their outdoor cooking to a new level. The book is full of great recipes, good humor and more information than most people will ever acquire on their own.

RETROGRADE has a great concept, but it’s poorly executed. The concept: The international (U.S., China, Russia, Eurasia) colony on Mars is prepared for absolutely everything that can go wrong on Mars, but is totally unprepared for anything to go wrong on Earth. So when nuclear war breaks out, with no one knowing who fired the first missile, the colonists are left in an impossible situation. They must cooperate to survive—their resupply ship has just sailed right on past Mars (failure of automated braking rockets)—but they don’t trust one another.

This is a wonderful plot idea, but the story gets bogged down by far too much detailed description of the layout, construction, and environment of the colony itself. Plus the characters talk, talk, talk about what alternative actions are available, and why each alternative won’t work (e.g., the Russians won’t go for it), but are very slow to start doing anything. When the characters aren’t discussing matters, and worrying about the fate of loved ones back on Earth, the lead character (Liz) is thinking about everything around her, and describing whatever is before her eyes in minute detail (e.g., the wheat growing in the common area shared by all the colonists).

To my mind, there simply isn’t enough action to drive the plot. I can believe that the detailed description of what a Mars colony will be like is technically and scientifically accurate (or as much as it can be in 2017), but it’s just too much information piled into a thin story. Also, I think the novel would be far better with a male lead, because Liz doesn’t ring true to me as a female researcher/adventurer.

In the novel, when it becomes clear what started Earth’s nuclear war, the plot becomes more interesting. However, the whole story has a hurried finish that needs an Epilogue to tie up the many loose ends, and in one important aspect the story has been done before.

The premise of this book is very straightforward and simple - each author describes the view from a window, either detailing the specifics of the view, describing the thoughts and revelations that the view brings or some combination on the two. Each view is presented in just one or two pages as most - just bite-sized nuggets of inspiring words to encourage one to observe the world from their own window. With each of these writings comes a pencil drawing that captures the view complete with its inspiring details and notable imperfections.

This is a unique collection of writings, based on an interesting premise and broken down into bite-sized chunks that make reading it easy and leisurely. This is a good book if you want to find inspiration in something that is often taken for granted - an everyday view from a window.

KING MAYBE, the fifth "Junior Bender" mystery, is a total delight for fans of the snarkily comic mystery genre. Timothy Hallinan is every bit as skilled at the genre as was the late Donald Westlake (author of [[ASIN:0446677035 The Hot Rock]] and [[ASIN:B005UK7U8A The Busy Body]]). I'm in awe of both writers, because writing a mystery that works perfectly as a mystery, while remaining genuinely humorous in tone, has got to be incredibly difficult.

KING MAYBE works fine as a standalone--it's my first "Junior Bender", and I loved everything about it (except for the clunky title). Junior is a professional burglar, and it's a tribute to his skills that he's never been caught. He's loveable as a boyfriend, as a divorced family man who's devoted to his daughter, as an honorable businessman who lives up to his contracts, and as a consummate pro who willingly shares his best burglar-trade secrets.

In the novel, Junior's fence (Stinky) hires him to steal a rare stamp. The job goes sideways when the stamp's owner, a fearsome gambling-debt collector (The Slugger), returns home unexpectedly. Junior gets away with the stamp, but only with unexpected help from his mysterious girl friend (Ronnie). Then he can't fence the stamp, because Stinky has gone into hiding after his houseboy was murdered.

Junior desperately needs money from the job, to pay off an old movie producer friend (Jake) who has hired a contract killer to do Junior. Then more and more problems surface. "Bad luck arrives on the wind," as Junior's mentor and surrogate father (Herbie) used to say; and the San Fernando Valley winds just won't stop blowing.

This is a fast read, a comic mystery novel with many unguessable plot twists, all neatly wrapped up and tied with a bow at the end. There are also many fun, interesting characters, including a couple of skilled hacker kids, a hit woman, a call girl, and a wheelchair-bound artist. I enjoyed every minute, and can't wait to read the remaining four Junior Bender mysteries.

We love pasta in our house and I have tried my hand a few times at making homemade pasta, with mixed results. I have other books on pasta and pasta-making and was interested in seeing how this one presents the subject. Some pasta books present nothing but formulas and methods for making the pasta itself; others present just ideas on how to cook pre-made pasta and prepare dishes with it. This book strikes a balance between the two.

This book is well-organized though I struggled with it initially. Most other pasta books I have seen have grouped all of the recipes and shaping/cutting methods together, then presents any recipes using those pastas with references back to the pastas themselves. This one is a bit different and is a bit of a hybrid when it comes to how it is organized. The first part of the book, consisting of two chapters, presents some introductory material as well as a primer of how to make pasta in a general sense (method without a recipe). Chapter three presents dough recipes without cutting and shaping methods attached. These recipes range from basic egg pasta to flavored doughs, whole wheat, gluten-free and more. The next 5 chapters present recipes and methods based primarily on pasta shapes, and the final chapter presents recipes for sauces and fillings.

The five chapters on shaped & cut pasta dishes is interesting. Each starts off with a “Learn and Make” introduction on how to make whatever pasta type is being presented, complete with detailed step-by-step instructions and multiple photographs detailing what to do along the way. This is outstanding and makes making each pasta type easy to understand and follow. The recipes that follow in the chapter then use the pasta presented (or a shaping variation of it) in the introductory part of the chapter.

Overall, this is a very instructional and well-organized collection.

One thing I would change, though – I would add more pictures to the recipe collection. The pasta preparation sections have plenty, but most dish recipes actually do not, and this makes it a little more difficult to pick a good dish out from the collection without looking for something specifically. The downside of adding more pictures is that the book would cost more due to higher production costs, but that would be offset by a more accessible collection.

I like this book and am happy to recommend it. It is filled with very instructional material on how to make good pasta at home, and it has a good collection of recipes that is well organized.

This is not my first exposure to a sugar detox plan. I have been through a near-complete sugar detox before and I can say from experience that the transformation you go through over the course of a couple of weeks is surprising in a number of ways. Contrary to what you might think, your energy level does climb (after an initial withdrawal crash) and your insatiable desire for sugar does fall off after a few days. Though the first few days are somewhat difficult, it’s really not that hard of a plan to follow. This book doesn’t follow a specific plan like Atkins or South Beach but it does provide a clear explanation of what is wrong with a high-sugar diet and provides a very good collection of recipes designed to help you stop the sugar craving cycle. That said, it isn’t accurate to call this book “sugar-free”.

The first couple of chapters have introductory material – why sugar is harmful to the body, what happens when we eat too much, and how to break the cycle and eat a diet with lower sugars. There is a two-week meal plan that provides a good, solid menu of how to get through the first two weeks of sugar elimination, a tool that is common in a lot of diet-related books.

The following chapters present recipes and ideas that fit into a variety of categories – breakfasts, snacks, main dishes and more. It’s not hard to find ideas in this book.

So, does this mean that this book presents a completely sugar-free lifestyle? Well, not exactly. Specifically, it avoids refined and high-concentration sugars like maple syrup, corn syrup, turbinado sugar, table sugars and more. It does not avoid things like fruits which have naturally-occurring sugars in them and as such are not strictly sugar-free. Also, you can find recipes in this book that rely on grains and other higher carbohydrate ingredients which of course the body metabolizes more quickly. To say that this book is a pure approach to a sugar-free lifestyle isn’t exactly accurate. It’s a step up from a typical American diet, regardless.

This is not a bad book and it presents a lot of good, better-for-you recipes than you’ll find in a “mainstream” cookbook. It slightly misrepresents itself by referring to a sugar-free lifestyle, though, as it more accurately describes a diet free of highly-refined and concentrated sugar foods.

FRIENDSHIP BREAD Release date: May 1, 2012 : In the tradition of Kate Jacobs and Lolly Winston comes a deeply felt, utterly charming novel of three newfound friends and the unexpected gift that will change their lives. In the quiet community of Avalon, Illinois, Julia Evarts wonders how to move on with her life. Though her husband and five-year-old daughter give her an abundance of love, Julia still reels from a tragedy that has left her estranged from the sister who was once her best friend. Meanwhile, across town, widow Madeleine Davis takes great pleasure in serving up delectable treats and cozy comforts at her tea salon--now, if only she had some customers to enjoy them. And famed concert cellist and recent Avalon transplant Hannah de Brisay finds herself at a crossroads when her career and marriage come to abrupt ends. The three strangers forge a friendship at Madeleine's Tea Shop, and soon their camaraderie extends to everyone in Avalon in the guise of a unique and wonderful gift. But even as Julia becomes ever closer to her new friends, she realizes the profound necessity of confronting the painful past she shares with her sister. Life and loss, friendship and community, food and family: Friendship Bread tells a spirited, remarkably moving tale about the triumph of hope. From Publishers Weekly: Baked goods conquer profound grief in Gee's by-the-numbers debut. The sorrow felt by Julia Evarts and her husband, Mark, over the death of their son, Josh, six years earlier has chipped away at the foundation of their marriage, but after Julia finds a starter batch of Amish friendship bread on her porch one day, the yeasty surprise helps patch up some spiritual wounds. She shares the recipe starter with a few people in her town, and pretty soon everyone is making it and finding their own simple narratives of bread-driven healing. But none have a harder path to the foregone conclusion than Julia and her sister, Livvy, who was with Josh when he died and has yet to be forgiven by Julia. Yes, the premise is hokey, but Gee's women characters are written with affection (much more so than the men in their lives, who are essentially decorative). Readers looking for a quick, easy fix of heartwarming optimism could do worse. And, of course, the recipe is included.

DEATH IN PROVENCE: A NOVEL (PENELOPE KITE) is a slow-moving cozy mystery with a drab, boring amateur detective (Penelope) and an uninteresting plot. Especially at the beginning, the narrative is weighed down by many untranslated French phrases that are presumably inserted to establish the Provence setting. I guess they’re needed, because other details regarding Penelope’s run-down stone cottage and its environs are fairly generic.

As for Penelope, she’s a middle-aged, divorced British ex-pat, with unappreciative step-children and horrible, insulting step-grandchildren back in England. She used to work for a medical examiner, which gives her limited forensic knowledge (e.g., the number of hours required for rigor mortis to wear off). She’s rather unsure of herself, which probably explains why local authorities don't take her very seriously when she shares her forensic theories about the murder of a local drunk found floating face down in her swimming pool. There's a love interest for Penelope, in the form of a dishy middle-aged mayor who seems to find her attractive.

The plot turns around some problems regarding the title to Penelope’s newly acquired dream home. Ownership became murky after WWII, when the property was first occupied by a French family suspected of collaborating with the Germans during the occupation. Penelope leans very heavily on the real estate agent (Clemence) who sold her the cottage. Clemence provides support far beyond what might be expected, including offering Penelope temporary shelter after the body is discovered, lining up repairmen, translating to supplement Penelope’s faltering French, and providing introductions to all the important local people.

Nothing about this novel makes me want to read any more of the series. Generally I love any and all cozy mysteries, but this one just falls flat.

I'm pretty picky about how good speakers perform. I'm not a hard nose audiophile, but I know good speakers when I hear them. I have used the same song for decades to truly test the quality of the bass. That song is Alan Parson's "The Raven" and the bass test is the very last note in the song. Most speaker systems cannot handle this deep bass guitar note at any volume. This set did. So as far as the bass, this speaker set passed the toughest test I could throw at it.

The high end was strong and clean, the midrange was the only level I saw a little lacking. This was playing music of the classic rock genre. I play my music pretty exclusively through Windows Media Player which offers a built-in equalizer. Just a little adjusting on the equalizer and I had all levels well balanced, sound was very good.

Some reviewers had mentioned hearing a hum or the like from the right speaker (the one which contains the power and volume controls). When I first hooked everything up out of the box I heard it too. It was noticeable and given time I could see it becoming irritating. I know what causes this hum and how to fix the problem. The problem is caused by poor shielding on the speaker wiring. I added 3 ft. extensions that were double shielded and lo and behold...no more hum, dead silence. I have since put 10 ft. double shielded extensions on both speakers and they are working flawlessly with zero degradation in performance. If you check the answered questions you will find the exact extensions you need. Be careful, not any VGA extension will work for the right speaker! Keep the original speaker wires away from any power cords or power sources and you should get the same result in the end.

CREATURES OF THE DEEP is a rarity among affordable coffee-table books--it has an excellent, readable text, in addition to beautiful photographs of creatures from all five layers of the sea.

Part One of the text describes a hypothetical descent from the ocean's surface to its floor, noting what the deep sea explorer will experience, see, and learn in each layer. The descent begins with the Epipelagic zone (e.g., whales); continues through the Mesopelagic zone (e.g., anglerfish, viperfish shown on cover), the Bathypelagic zone (e.g., vampire squid, cold water corals), and the Abyssopelagic zone (e.g., giant squid); until it ends with the Hadal zone (e.g., sea cucumber). My favorite section is the description of the deepest zone, which also includes accounts of famous deep-sea researchers and bathyscaphe explorations.

Part Two focuses on specific sea creatures (sharks, plankton, copepods, jellyfish, squid, whales, dragonfish), and the ocean-dweller food chain.

Part Three discusses tectonic plates, ocean mountain ranges, and hydrothermal vents (plus the creatures living there (e.g., tubeworms, vent shrimp, microbes and other microorganisms)).

Part Four describes marine life census projects (tagging predators, identifying new species), the conservation of sea creatures' habitats, and the conservation of oceans in general.

If this book inspires you or someone in your family to learn more, you might consider these other beautiful coffee-table-sized books: [[ASIN:0226595668 The Deep: The Extraordinary Creatures of the Abyss]] (rare photos of deep-sea creatures, with page-margin hash marks showing the ocean zone that harbors each creature); [[ASIN:0756636922 Ocean: The World's Last Wilderness Revealed]] (a Cousteau factoid book filled with information about the oceans; photos of plants, fish, and everything else that lives in the sea; and descriptions of many, many ocean species); and [[ASIN:1552979997 Oceanic Wilderness]] (a huge book with lovely fish photos taken on underwater dives, now remaindered).

Received this one as a gift.  What a nice surprise it turned out to be.  With Have a Little Faith, Michael Elliott has delivered a John Hiatt bio that reads like a fine Hiatt LP.  It's concise, observational, to-the-point, revels in clever turns-of-phrase, and finds hope and truth in the simple yet complex ways the road of life takes us.  It reads like a series of time-tested classic Hiatt compositions.  Like a lot of folks, I came to Hiatt first by covers (Three Dog Night's Sure as I'm Sitting Here, Bonnie Raitt's Thing Called Love, Desert Rose Band's She Don't Love Nobody), then by his career changing Bring the Family LP.  And what a wonderful career it has turned out to be!  But the backstories are deep and wide, and Hiatt has survived and thrived over many a heartbreak and setback.  You don't have to know all of his music to enjoy this read, but it helps to have a handle on the most important among his songs and albums.  One story in particular really hit me: When he's in Elvis Presley's Rolls and kind of breaks into tears, explaining it was because he realized "just how trapped he was ...  Just trapped.  He was just a poor mama's boy from Mississippi."  As a lifelong fan of Elvis, I could truly relate to John Hiatt's humanity in this special moment.  Riding with the King, indeed.  Highly recommended.

The Keto Diet has been around for a while but has enjoyed a bit of popularity since the low-carb diet wave hit. One of the hardest things to give up on such diets is carbohydrates, and this cookbook sets out to bridge the gap and make the transition easier.

Many substitutions are required to make a conversion like this and you’ll find bunches of them in the recipes - such things as coconut flour, monk fruit extract, riced cauliflower, and more. This is true of just about any keto or low-carb book so this is nothing new, but if you’re not expecting this it can come as a shock. These substitutions make the recipes work like “normal” recipes that have flour and sugar and other high-carb foods like potatoes.

So, what kinds of things can you find in this cookbook? Such things as jelly-filled doughnuts, waffles and pancakes, breaded and fried things like avocado fries and sesame crackers, pizzas and sandwiches, pasta dishes (often using “zoodles”), rice-based dishes that have no rice, desserts like cookies, and even breads. Yes, these do turn out differently than their traditional equivalents, but they are close enough to work and to satisfy the cravings.

I haven’t made a lot of these yet but those I have tried have turned out better than I expected. I wouldn’t know they were lower carb dishes without having prepared them myself or without being told. And, the recipes are easy!

Each recipe has a series of tags across the top that highlight recipe features such as “30 Minutes or Less”, “Dairy Free”, and “Vegetarian”, to name a few. What is interesting is that there are vegan dishes in the collection that are not specifically labeled as vegan, just vegetarian (a good example of this is the recipe for Cauliflower Rice on page 108, which has just salt, olive oil and cauliflower). This might be a missed opportunity for people looking into keto recipes that are vegan in nature; it would be easy to miss this recipe and not realize it works.

This is a nice starter book for keto cooking, particularly for those who cannot give up their carbs. The recipes are easy to follow and turn out good.

I make a lot of bread and I have recently decided to concentrate on whole grain artisan loaves. I found this title on a shelf and decided to give it a chance.

The subtitle of this book is "Baking with Whole Grains". Based on this, one would be led to believe that a typical recipe from this book would be very much based on whole grains, be it wheat flour, rye, or cornmeal. Unfortunately, a good percentage of the recipes in the book come off as normal recipes based on highly refined flours, with a little whole grain goodness added in just to meet the criteria of the subtitle. Perhaps this meets the requirements to the letter, but it seems that it violates the spirit of the idea of whole-grain baking.

For "real" whole-grain baked goods, there are better choices in cookbooks.

So, in spite of this issue, the recipes within are actually quite good! I have made several of these and my family has been very pleased. Perhaps the most interesting surprise from this book has been "Skillet Custard Cornbread", a cornbread with a soft custard layer on top, baked in a cast-iron skillet. The breakfast breads (pancakes, waffles, etc) are also exceptional and are among the more requested things I make for my family now.

While this book is not the whole-grain baking book I had hoped for, it is still full of good recipes and I will use it regularly. I cannot give it 5 stars because of the deceptive title; if you can find a copy on a shelf somewhere, take a look at it before you decide to buy. If its shortcoming is something you can overlook, it is still a very good bread/baking book in its own right.
